title: The Verbal Sentence: Past Tense & كَانَ

steps.title: A sentence that starts with a verb
body: Every sentence so far has been nominal — a topic next to a comment, no verb, no word for "is". Arabic has a second sentence type too, and it starts with a verb: فِعْل – فَاعِل – مَفْعُول (verb – subject – object). ذَهَبَ الرَّجُلُ ("went the-man") is completely normal Arabic — the subject comes after the verb, not before it. A subject-first order is also fine, especially for emphasis, but verb-first is the neutral default.

The verb itself changes its ending for the person doing the action — the same ending pattern works on any Form I verb you already know: هُوَ ذَهَبَ، هِيَ ذَهَبَتْ، هُمْ ذَهَبُوا، أَنَا ذَهَبْتُ، أَنْتَ ذَهَبْتَ، أَنْتِ ذَهَبْتِ، نَحْنُ ذَهَبْنَا. Every "to X" word you've learned is already the "he did X" form — dhahaba doesn't just mean "to go", it means "he went".

There's one more piece: كَانَ ("was / were") takes a nominal sentence into the past. الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ (the house is big) becomes كَانَ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرًا (the house was big) — and the description afterward switches from ـٌ to ـًا. كان conjugates irregularly, so كَانَ، كَانَتْ، كَانُوا، كُنْتُ are worth learning as their own small set.

steps.title: Verbs first, then كان
steps.intro: Read each sentence aloud. The first three are plain past tense; the last three use كان. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: Verb, then subject

options.label: Verb first, then subject — Arabic's neutral order (VSO)
Subject first, then verb, the way English works
There's no subject in this sentence

steps.explanation: ذَهَبَ (the verb) comes before الرَّجُلُ (the subject) — verb-subject-object is Arabic's default, unlike English.

steps.title: Who's speaking?
steps.prompt: Which ending tells you who did the going?
steps.explanation: ذَهَبْتُ (dhahabtu) is the same root, ذهب, with the ـتُ ending — that ending alone means "I", no separate word needed.

steps.title: Why كَبِيرًا, not كَبِيرٌ?
steps.prompt: Why does the description end in ـًا here instead of the ـٌ a plain nominal sentence would use?

options.label: Because خَبَر كَانَ (كان's comment) is accusative, not nominative
ـًا and ـٌ are interchangeable spellings of the same thing

steps.explanation: كان pushes its comment into the accusative case — الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ (nominal sentence) becomes كَانَ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرًا once كان makes it past tense.

steps.title: You can read Arabic's other sentence type
steps.message: You've now seen both of Arabic's sentence types: nominal (topic + comment, no verb) and verbal (verb first, then subject). You conjugated a Form I verb across all seven persons in the past tense, and used كَانَ to put a description in the past — including its own irregular conjugation.
